summary:
FIREBALL is a web-based Microgravity Combustion Intelligence System developed for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It helps users explore microgravity combustion research, compare findings, and generate AI-assisted scientific syntheses linked to supporting evidence.

The platform addresses the challenge by turning dispersed research into an accessible, structured resource for understanding how fire behaves in microgravity. Its interface connects scientific findings with questions relevant to spacecraft fire safety, while highlighting evidence gaps, uncertainty, and the limits of available studies.

Understanding combustion beyond Earth is essential to protecting crews and designing safer space habitats. FIREBALL supports this goal by making complex research easier to navigate and interpret, helping users identify relevant evidence and questions for further investigation. The result is a research prototype that bridges scientific literature and mission-oriented exploration.
details:
FIREBALL is a web-based Microgravity Combustion Intelligence Platform that I developed independently for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It brings scientific evidence, experimental comparisons, and research signal forecasting into one interface to help users investigate combustion in microgravity.

What it does and how it works

The platform contains four main sections:

• Overview introduces reviewed scientific findings, their research implications, and their limitations. It gives users a starting point for exploring the available combustion evidence.

• Combustion Analysis allows users to select documented trials and compare their recorded conditions. The comparison distinguishes differences in reported values from missing information. It also makes clear that matching conditions alone do not establish a controlled experiment or a causal relationship.

• Predictive Engine lets users select a recorded source channel and a forecast horizon within one Saffire-II case. It evaluates research forecasts against a persistence baseline and displays test error. These results describe performance within a chronological test block from one trial, rather than validation across independent flights.

• Scientific Intelligence supports research questions and comparisons of reviewed evidence. Its optional AI generation produces question-specific scientific drafts with source identifiers and references. AI generation currently requires an access code, while the public workspace remains available for exploration. Generated drafts require review against the original publications.

Benefits and intended impact

FIREBALL helps users navigate research while keeping experimental context visible. Instead of presenting every numerical result as directly comparable, it highlights differences in materials, geometry, flow orientation, and reported outcomes.

My intended impact is to support research exploration relevant to spacecraft fire safety, help users identify evidence gaps, and make complex findings more accessible. The platform remains a research prototype and is not validated for operational fire-safety decisions.

Development tools

I built FIREBALL using Python and Streamlit, with Pandas and NumPy for data handling and Plotly for interactive visualization. I used GitHub for source-code hosting and Streamlit Community Cloud to publish the application. I developed the project on a personal laptop.

Creative approach and design considerations

The creative contribution is the integration of evidence exploration, trial comparison, and signal forecasting in one research workflow. The interface combines an aerospace-inspired visual identity with explicit information about uncertainty and evidence limits.

As the sole developer, I prioritized traceability, public accessibility, clear separation between documented findings and generated interpretation, and honest communication of model limitations. I also considered limited computing resources and API usage, which informed the lightweight web implementation and restricted access to optional AI generation.
